title: Someone got Doom in an SQL database
gist: Lukas Vogel's SQLDoom renders full-color 640x480 Doom frames entirely through about 1,300 lines of SQL in CedarDB, reaching roughly 60 fps on a Ryzen 7 laptop. It is a novelty project, but it shows a relational database handling real-time game state and rendering, with multiplayer consistency as the claimed practical benefit.

insights.claim: SQLDoom implements Doom's game logic and rendering with about 1,300 lines of SQL across 89 common table expressions in CedarDB, producing 35 bitmap framebuffers per second, with only a small Python client handling input, output and timing.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Shows a modern analytical SQL engine can run a real-time workload far outside its design brief, a signal of CedarDB's performance.
insights.quote: about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second
insights.locator: Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables

insights.claim: SQLDoom upgrades Vogel's earlier DoomQL, which produced raycast grayscale ASCII graphics, to full-color 640x480 frames that resemble the original Doom executable's output.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Rapid year-over-year jump in what SQL-only rendering can do indicates the database engine, not the idea, was the bottleneck.
insights.locator: In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement

insights.claim: Vogel reports about 60 fps on a Ryzen 7 laptop despite the overhead of reading and writing SQL tables for everything, with dips to 35 fps in busy scenes.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Consumer-grade hardware suffices, so the performance headroom of database engines is larger than commonly assumed.

themes.theme: Mapping game data to relational form

insights.claim: Doom's WAD files convert to relational tables easily because levels are already decomposed into vertices, lines and sectors.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Data models that are already structured and normalized port to databases cheaply, which favors database-native designs.

insights.claim: Precomputing a sort_key for each object at load time lets a plain ORDER BY replace Doom's binary-space-partition traversal, deciding each frame which wall parts to draw and vastly improving performance.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Shifting computation to load time and leaning on the database's sort is the key trick for making SQL viable in real-time workloads.
insights.locator: Even Doom's famous binary-space partition trees

insights.claim: Floors and ceilings were the hardest part, because Doom's visplanes and state mutations do not map to SQL, so Vogel used a self-described hacky replacement that iterates over an ordered list of panels.
insights.speaker: Lukas Vogel
insights.so_what: Stateful, mutation-heavy algorithms are where set-based SQL strains, which limits its generality.

insights.claim: Vogel argues a database holding a steady reference snapshot of game state, plus built-in concurrency and access handling, benefits multiplayer servers by avoiding partially applied updates, physics bugs and disputes over hits.
insights.speaker: Lukas Vogel
insights.so_what: Transactional guarantees as a game-state layer is a niche idea; watch whether any real multiplayer backends adopt it.
insights.quote: no partially applied updates, physics bugs, or disagreements over whether the rocket actually hit

insights.claim: Vogel concedes that rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea, so the project is a showcase of capability rather than a recommended architecture.
insights.speaker: Lukas Vogel
insights.so_what: Treat it as a marketing and benchmark demo for CedarDB rather than a commercial use case.
insights.quote: Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea

insights.claim: The hosted online demo gave the author poor performance, while local setup needs only the GitHub code, CedarDB and a Doom WAD file.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Performance shown on a local laptop may not carry over to shared hosted infrastructure.
insights.locator: If you want to run a Doomtabase
